In the high-frequency AC regime, orientational relaxation is governed by induced dipoles, and the observed memory effect originates from polydispersity, which generates a spectrum of rotational diffusion coefficients and hence multiscale relaxation. Building on this insight, we design protocols that mitigate the detrimental effect of memory by sequentially suppressing the slowest active relaxation mode. Experiments on nanoparticle suspensions with different properties confirm these mechanisms, and we demonstrate substantial reductions in relaxation time compared with single quenches and matched two-step protocols with NaMt suspensions. More broadly, these results illustrate how memory effects emerge when many degrees of freedom are steered with a single control parameter and provide an experimentally accessible strategy for controlling multiscale stochastic dynamics.
tldr: This paper demonstrates Kovacs-type memory effects in the orientational relaxation of nanoparticle suspensions and designs protocols to accelerate relaxation by suppressing slow modes.
motivation: Understanding and overcoming memory effects that limit acceleration of relaxation in stochastic systems is important for controlling multiscale dynamics.
method: Optical birefringence measurements of field-induced orientation in polydisperse nanoparticle suspensions, combined with Smoluchowski equation modeling and multi-step field protocols.
result: Kovacs nonmonotonic relaxation is observed and attributed to polydispersity; sequential suppression of slow modes reduces relaxation time significantly.
conclusion: Memory effects in polydisperse systems can be mitigated by tailored multi-step protocols, providing a strategy for accelerating relaxation in soft matter.

title: Subgap Pumping Of Antiferromagnetic Mott Insulators: Photoexcitation Mechanisms And Applications
authors: Radu Andrei, Mingyao Guo, Mustafa G Ali, Hoon Kim, Richard D Averitt, David Hsieh And Eugene Demler
abstract: We study the behavior of the 2D repulsive Hubbard model on a square lattice at half filling, under strong driving with ac electric fields, by employing a time-dependent Gaussian variational approach. Within the same theoretical framework, we analytically obtain the conventional Keldysh crossover between multiphoton and tunneling photoexcitation mechanisms, as well as two new regimes beyond the Keldysh paradigm. We discuss how dynamical renormalization of the Mott–Hubbard gap feeds back into the photoexcitation process, modulating the carrier generation rate in real time. The momentum distribution of quasiparticle excitations immediately after the drive is calculated, and shown to contain valuable information about the generation mechanism. Finally, we discuss experimental probing of the pump-induced nonequilibrium electronic state.
tldr: The paper studies photoexcitation mechanisms in antiferromagnetic Mott insulators under strong ac driving, revealing regimes beyond the Keldysh crossover and dynamical gap renormalization.
motivation: Understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated systems under intense light is crucial for controlling electronic phases and developing ultrafast optoelectronics.
method: A time-dependent Gaussian variational approach is applied to the 2D repulsive Hubbard model at half filling to simulate the response to ac electric fields.
result: Analytical derivation of conventional Keldysh crossover and two new photoexcitation regimes; dynamical renormalization of the Mott gap modulates carrier generation; momentum distribution of quasiparticles reveals generation mechanism.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for photoexcitation in Mott insulators and suggests experimental probes to access the non-equilibrium electronic state.

title: Quantum Entanglement, Stratified Spaces, And Topological Matter: Towards Entanglement-sensitive Langlands Data
authors: Kazuki Ikeda And Steven Rayan
abstract: Using the spinless Haldane model, we study the witness-filtered Berry curvature, quantum geometric tensor, and quantum Fisher information on the gapped strata of the parameter space and evaluate them through the Fukui–Hatsugai–Suzuki discretization. The filtered quantities isolate the part of the geometric response carried by sublattice coherence: they suppress contributions from regions where the occupied Bloch state is locally A/B-separable and emphasize regions where curvature and coherence coexist. We derive exact lattice identities, reconstruction formulas for the curvature-weighted coherence, and bounds relating the filtered quantum geometric tensor and quantum Fisher information to single-particle mode entanglement. Across the gap-closing stratum, the quantized response changes admit a natural description in terms of Hecke modifications. We elicit a corresponding Langlands viewpoint—not as a full correspondence, but as an organizational principle and as the mathematical shadow of these physical geometric constructions.
tldr: The paper uses the Haldane model to study filtered geometric quantities and connects them to entanglement and Langlands theory.
motivation: To isolate geometric response due to sublattice coherence and relate it to entanglement in topological matter.
method: Applies witness-filtered Berry curvature, quantum geometric tensor, and quantum Fisher information on gapped strata using Fukui–Hatsugai–Suzuki discretization.
result: Derives exact lattice identities, bounds linking filtered geometric tensors to single-particle mode entanglement, and describes quantized response changes via Hecke modifications.
conclusion: The Langlands viewpoint serves as an organizational principle for these physical geometric constructions.

title: Quantum Cellular Automata On Symmetric Subalgebras
authors: Ruochen Ma, Yabo Li, And Meng Cheng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2123 (2026).

We investigate quantum cellular automata (QCA) on one-dimensional spin systems defined over a subalgebra of the full local operator algebra – the symmetric subalgebra under a finite Abelian group symmetry [MATH]. For systems where each site carries a regular representation of [MATH], we establish a complete classification of such subalgebra QCAs based on two topological invariants: (1) a surjective homomorphism from the group of subalgebra QCAs to the group of anyon permutation symmetries in a [MATH] [MATH] gauge theory; and (2) a generalization of the Gross-Nesme-Vogts-Werner (GNVW) index that characterizes the flow of the symmetric subalgebra. Specifically, two subalgebra QCAs correspond to the same anyon permutation and share the same index if and only if they differ by a finite-depth unitary circuit composed of [MATH]-symmetric local gates. We also identify a set of operations that generate all subalgebra QCAs through finite compositions. As an example, we examine the Kramers-Wannier duality on a [MATH] symmetric subalgebra, demonstrating that it maps to the [MATH]-[MATH] permutation in the two-dimensional toric code and has an irrational index of [MATH]. Therefore, it cannot be extended to a QCA over the full local operator algebra and mixes nontrivially with lattice translations.

.
tldr: Classifies quantum cellular automata on symmetric subalgebras using topological invariants and shows the Kramers-Wannier duality has irrational index.
motivation: To understand the structure and classification of quantum cellular automata that preserve a symmetry subalgebra, which is a topic in quantum computation theory.
method: Uses algebraic methods to define two topological invariants: an anyon permutation map and a generalized GNVW index, and proves that these classify subalgebra QCAs up to finite-depth symmetric circuits.
result: Establishes a complete classification of subalgebra QCAs on one-dimensional spin systems with finite Abelian group symmetry, and demonstrates that the Kramers-Wannier duality corresponds to a nontrivial anyon permutation and has irrational index.
conclusion: Subalgebra QCAs are strictly richer than full-algebra QCAs and cannot be extended to the full algebra, mixing nontrivially with translations.

title: Squeezing Enhancement In Lossy Multi-Path Atom Interferometers
authors: Julian Günther, Jan-Niclas Kirsten-Siemß, Naceur Gaaloul, And Klemens Hammerer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2122 (2026).

This paper explores the sensitivity gains afforded by spin-squeezed states in atom interferometry, in particular using Bragg diffraction. We introduce a generalised input-output formalism that accurately describes realistic, non-unitary interferometers, including losses due to velocity selectivity and scattering into undesired momentum states. This formalism is applied to evaluate the performance of one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states in improving phase sensitivity. Our results show that by carefully optimising the parameters of the Bragg beam splitters and controlling the degree of squeezing, it is possible to improve the sensitivity of the interferometer by several dB with respect to the standard quantum limit despite realistic levels of losses in light pulse operations. However, the analysis also highlights the challenges associated with achieving these improvements in practice, most notably the impact of finite temperature on the benefits of entanglement. The results suggest ways of optimising interferometric setups to exploit quantum entanglement under realistic conditions, thereby contributing to advances in precision metrology with atom interferometers.

.
tldr: This paper studies sensitivity enhancement using spin-squeezed states in lossy multi-path atom interferometers, focusing on practical metrology.
motivation: Atom interferometry is limited by the standard quantum limit; spin-squeezed states can surpass it, but losses and finite temperature degrade performance.
method: A generalized input-output formalism is developed to model non-unitary interferometers with losses, and one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states are evaluated.
result: Optimizing Bragg beam splitter parameters and squeezing degree yields several dB improvement over the standard quantum limit despite losses.
conclusion: Quantum entanglement can enhance atom interferometry under realistic conditions, but finite temperature remains a significant challenge.

title: Hidden Time-nonlocal Floquet Symmetries
authors: Sigmund Kohler And Jesús Casado-Pascual
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2112 (2026).

We investigate the Floquet spectrum of a detuned, driven two-level system and show that it exhibits exact quasienergy crossings when the detuning is an integer multiple of the energy quantum of the driving field. This behavior can be explained by a hidden time-nonlocal parity, which allows the Floquet modes to be classified as even or odd. Then a generic feature is the emergence of exact crossings between quasienergies of different parity. A constructive proof of the existence of the symmetry is based on a scalar recurrence relation. Moreover, we present a general scheme for its numerical computation, which can be applied to models beyond the two-level system. Analytical results are illustrated with numerical data.

.
tldr: The paper studies hidden time-nonlocal Floquet symmetries in driven two-level systems, explaining exact quasienergy crossings via a parity classification.
motivation: Understanding exact quasienergy crossings in Floquet systems is important for controlling quantum dynamics, but the paper focuses on a specific symmetry property rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The authors use a scalar recurrence relation to construct a hidden time-nonlocal parity operator and numerically compute it for models beyond two-level systems.
result: Exact quasienergy crossings occur when detuning is an integer multiple of the driving quantum, and these crossings are protected by the hidden parity symmetry.
conclusion: The hidden symmetry provides a classification of Floquet modes and explains generic crossing features, but the work is primarily about Floquet theory and symmetry, not directly related to the user's research directions.

motivation: Solid-state platforms for continuously tuning chaotic dynamics have been lacking, which limits applications in mesoscopic physics and quantum information.

result: They achieve controlled transition from regular to chaotic dynamics by varying cavity shape, observing signatures of quantum chaos in transport and spectral measurements.
conclusion: Bilayer graphene cavities provide a tunable platform for studying quantum chaos, with potential implications for wavefunction engineering and quantum information.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: Presents an open-source Python library for optical layout and modular baseplates for AMO experiments, demonstrated with trapped-ion qubit gates.
motivation: Complex optical design in quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions is not scalable due to conventional piecewise setup.
method: Develops PyOpticL, a Python library using beam-path simulation and dynamic routing, and creates modular drop-in baseplates for common optical subsystems.
result: Demonstrates a full laser system for strontium trapped ions achieving over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates.
conclusion: Enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems, fostering open-source collaborative hardware design.

title: Bosonic Content Of Three-fermion Highest-spin States
authors: Jerzy Cioslowski, Krzysztof Strasburger, And Denis K. Sunko
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2121 (2026).

A rigorous characterization of the information content of any highest-spin three-fermion wave function is presented. It is based upon a formal decomposition of the wave function into a finite set of fixed invariants, called shapes, whose sole purpose is to satisfy the Pauli principle, and a variable part, constituting the bosonic excitations of these invariants, that provides its physical content. As an example, this decomposition is applied to a benchmark-quality approximate wave function of the lowest-energy quartet electronic state of the lithium atom. This wave function, which comprises hundreds of basis functions, is reduced to eleven shape blocks, only five of which are numerically significant. Such a compact characterization is a generic example of the appearance of superselection rules in configuration space, and provides a qualitative aid in the search for robust few-particle entangled states.

.
tldr: This paper decomposes three-fermion highest-spin wave functions into shape invariants and bosonic excitations, applied to the lithium atom.
motivation: To characterize the information content of fermionic wave functions and identify robust few-particle entangled states.
method: Formal decomposition of the wave function into fixed invariants (shapes) satisfying the Pauli principle and a variable bosonic part.
result: A benchmark lithium wave function with hundreds of basis functions is reduced to eleven shape blocks, five of which are numerically significant.
conclusion: The decomposition reveals superselection rules in configuration space and aids in finding robust entangled states.

title: Anisotropic Fluorescence Signals Retarded Dipole-dipole Interactions In A Thermal Atomic Cloud
authors: Vyacheslav Shatokhin, Friedemann Landmesser, Mario Niebuhr, Frank Stienkemeier, Andreas Buchleitner And Lukas Bruder
abstract: We experimentally observe and theoretically explain anisotropic multiple quantum coherence signals in the fluorescence from dilute thermal potassium vapours, at room temperature and particle densities . We identify the retarded part of the geometrically fully resolved inter-atomic, resonant dipole-dipole interaction as the crucial ingredient to theoretically reproduce all qualitative features of the experimental spectra.
tldr: Experimental and theoretical study of anisotropic fluorescence signals from thermal atomic vapors due to retarded dipole-dipole interactions.
motivation: To understand the role of retarded dipole-dipole interactions in many-body systems and their manifestation in fluorescence signals.
method: Combined experimental measurements on thermal potassium vapors with theoretical modeling of retarded dipole-dipole interactions.
result: Retarded dipole-dipole interactions are crucial to reproduce the observed anisotropic multiple quantum coherence signals.
conclusion: The work provides insight into light-matter interactions in dense atomic ensembles, relevant for quantum optics and atomic physics.

title: Percolation With Coupled Lasers: Effect Of Non-linearities On The Phase Transition
authors: Simon Mahler, Nikita Stroev, Mahmoud Abu Rmilah, Asher Friesem And Nir Davidson
abstract: Controlled experimental studies of percolation are challenging due to difficulties in tuning site connectivity, isolating local interactions, and mitigating finite-size effects. In this work, we experimentally investigate percolation with a platform of coupled lasers, where connectivity, interaction strength, and system size can be controlled. Using a square array of lasers with astronomical number of possible cluster configurations, we show that the emergence of a percolating cluster corresponds to the onset of phase locking among the lasers. We also show that the percolation probability undergoes a second-order alike transition as a function of the site-occupation probability, with a threshold consistent with classical theoretical predictions. Surprisingly, we find that at low pump level, amplified mode competition (nonlinear regime) alters the effective behavior of the lasing sites and modify the nature of the percolation transition. The experimental results are interpreted by the means of a theoretical toy model with connectivity rules to the classical percolation.
tldr: This paper experimentally studies percolation using a coupled laser array, showing that the percolation transition corresponds to phase locking and that nonlinearities modify the transition.
motivation: Controlled experimental studies of percolation are difficult; coupled lasers offer tunable connectivity and system size to study percolation phenomena.
method: A square array of coupled lasers is used to realize percolation, with site-occupation probability controlled by pump levels. Phase locking is measured to identify percolation clusters.
result: The percolation probability undergoes a second-order-like transition consistent with classical percolation theory, but nonlinearities at low pump levels alter the effective behavior and transition nature.
conclusion: Coupled lasers provide a versatile platform for studying percolation, and nonlinear effects can modify the phase transition, offering insights into complex systems.

title: Nonreciprocal Electrical Transport In Emerging Noncentrosymmetric Systems: From Hidden Symmetry To Functional Devices
authors: Shengyao Li, Zherui Yang, Xueyan Wang, Kian Ping Loh And X Renshaw Wang
abstract: Contrary to the reciprocal electrical transport constrained by the Onsager relations, nonreciprocal electrical transport arises in noncentrosymmetric systems where the resistance depends on the direction of current flow or external stimuli such as a magnetic field. Governed by symmetry-dependent charge dynamics, these responses appear as nonreciprocal charge transport (NCT) in the longitudinal direction and the nonlinear Hall effect (NLHE) in the transverse direction. Recent theoretical advances have expanded the range of mechanisms and material platforms capable of hosting nonreciprocal signals, revealing the role of hidden band-geometric properties. In parallel, experimental developments have exploited these effects for practical devices, offering promising alternatives to semiconductor-based rectifiers and wireless components, with advantages in broadband operation, ultrafast response, and high energy efficiency. In this review, we summarize electrical measurement techniques and characteristic transport signatures for identifying nonreciprocal phenomena and uncovering their underlying symmetry. We provide a comprehensive discussion of the fundamental mechanisms underlying NCT and NLHE, organized through representative material systems, and a subsequent examination of strategies for artificially inducing and enhancing nonreciprocity. Finally, we evaluate the technological perspectives of nonreciprocal electrical transport for electronic applications, along with key challenges and opportunities for scalable device implementation. By synthesizing current progress, this review aims to guide materials discovery and device innovation, and to inspire exploration of new symmetry settings and unconventional routes toward enhanced nonreciprocal functionalities.
tldr: A review of nonreciprocal electrical transport in noncentrosymmetric systems, focusing on symmetry-dependent charge dynamics and device applications.
motivation: To understand and exploit nonreciprocal transport phenomena for novel electronic devices beyond conventional semiconductors.
method: Summarizes theoretical mechanisms (band-geometric properties) and experimental techniques for measuring nonreciprocal charge transport and nonlinear Hall effect.
result: Identifies material platforms and strategies to induce/enhance nonreciprocity, with potential for broadband, ultrafast, energy-efficient rectifiers and wireless components.
conclusion: Nonreciprocal transport offers promising device functionalities, but challenges remain in scalable implementation and materials discovery.

title: Crystallography-driven Molecularization Of A Two-dimensional Spin- 3 / ...
authors: Hari Borutta, Tobias Müller, Ronny Thomale, Harald O Jeschke And Yasir Iqbal
abstract: Large-spin two-dimensional magnets are generally expected to develop conventional long-range order once the dominant exchange scale becomes appreciable. The layered spin- maple-leaf compound Na Mn O defies this expectation: despite sizable antiferromagnetic interactions and no evident disorder, it exhibits no magnetic ordering and displays two well-separated thermodynamic crossover scales. We show that this behavior originates from a crystallography-driven molecularization of the magnetic degrees of freedom. The low-symmetry structure partitions the Mn sublattice into inequivalent exchange pathways, generating a pronounced hierarchy that nearly isolates antiferromagnetic hexagons. Magnetic correlations therefore develop in two stages: first within individual hexagons at a scale set by the dominant exchange, and only at much lower temperatures do frustrated inter-hexagon couplings attempt to establish coherence across the lattice. While isolated hexagons reproduce the two-step thermodynamic structure, the experimentally relevant temperature scales emerge only once the hexagons are embedded in the frustrated two-dimensional network. The resulting quantum ground state is magnetically disordered, characterized by strong intra-hexagon correlations and rapidly decaying inter-hexagon correlations. These results identify crystallographic inequivalence as a materials-level mechanism for stabilizing molecularized and quantum-disordered states even in large-spin two-dimensional magnets.
tldr: This paper explains the absence of magnetic order in a large-spin 2D magnet via crystallography-driven molecularization into weakly coupled antiferromagnetic hexagons.
motivation: To understand why the layered spin-3/2 compound NaMn2O4 does not order magnetically despite strong antiferromagnetic interactions and no disorder.
method: The authors perform electronic structure calculations and model the magnetic system as a Heisenberg model on a maple-leaf lattice, analyzing exchange hierarchies and using exact diagonalization and classical Monte Carlo.
result: The low-symmetry structure creates a hierarchy of exchanges that nearly isolates antiferromagnetic hexagons, leading to two-stage magnetic correlations and a quantum disordered ground state.
conclusion: Crystallographic inequivalence can stabilize molecularized and quantum-disordered states in large-spin 2D magnets, offering a new materials-level mechanism.

title: Kovacs-like Memory Effect In Strain Stiffening Collagen Networks
authors: Maitri Mandal And Sayantan Majumdar Abhishek Ghadai
abstract: Materials driven far from equilibrium can encode memories of past deformations through long-lived structural reorganizations. Such memory effects-reflecting parameters such as deformation direction, magnitude, and duration have been widely explored in soft amorphous solids. Here, we report a Kovacs-like memory effect manifested as a non-monotonic stress relaxation in vitro biopolymer networks formed by type-I collagen, an essential component of the mammalian extracellular matrix. Using shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging, we find that this memory effect emerges exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, and persists over a much broader range of strain amplitudes than previously reported for other viscoelastic amorphous materials. Furthermore, we uncover a strong correlation between the memory response and the development of negative normal stresses and associated strain fields, highlighting the unique nonequilibrium mechanics underlying memory formation in biopolymer networks.
tldr: This paper reports a Kovacs-like memory effect in strain-stiffening collagen networks, focusing on non-equilibrium mechanics of biopolymer networks.
motivation: To understand memory effects in soft amorphous materials, specifically in biopolymer networks like collagen, which are important for biological tissues.
method: Shear rheology combined with in-situ optical imaging to measure stress relaxation and normal stresses in collagen networks under nonlinear strain-stiffening conditions.
result: A non-monotonic stress relaxation (Kovacs-like memory effect) is observed exclusively in the nonlinear strain-stiffening regime, correlated with negative normal stresses.
conclusion: The memory effect in collagen networks arises from unique nonequilibrium mechanics distinct from other amorphous materials, with implications for biological tissue mechanics.

title: Continuous Thermochemical Sources Of AlF Molecules
authors: Pulkit Kukreja, Priyansh Agarwal, Maximilian Doppelbauer, Jionghao Cai, Xiangyue Liu, Eduardo Padilla, Sebastian Kray, Henrik Haak, Russell Thomas, Stefan Truppe, Boris G Sartakov, Gerard Meijer And Sid Wright
abstract: The AlF molecule, currently subject to laser cooling and trapping efforts, has the advantage that it can be efficiently produced in a thermochemical reaction between sublimated aluminum trifluoride and aluminum metal. Here we present a series of experiments with continuous molecular beam sources of AlF, utilizing this reaction. We demonstrate a compact AlF molecular beam oven whose total far-field brightness is molecules per steradian per second at 923 K, just below the melting temperature of aluminum metal. The continuous output from the oven begins to exceed the peak brightness of a jet-cooled, ablation-based supersonic AlF source for the , level, and we obtain an excellent signal-to-noise ratio with the oven in pulsed laser ionization spectroscopy experiments. By delivering flux from the oven into a cryogenic Ne buffer gas cell, we lower the rotational temperature of the beam to around 30 K and reduce its most probable forward velocity from 600 m s to 200 m s . In addition, we demonstrate that AlF can be made in a simple dispenser package, and observe that molecules thermalize to the laboratory temperature after colliding with vacuum chamber walls of the experiment. The resulting transient AlF vapor may enable direct loading of a molecular magneto-optical trap.
tldr: This paper presents experimental demonstrations of continuous thermochemical sources for producing AlF molecules, focusing on molecular beam brightness and cooling for laser cooling and trapping.
motivation: AlF molecules are promising for laser cooling and trapping, but efficient and continuous sources are needed for advanced experiments.
method: The authors use a thermochemical reaction between sublimated aluminum trifluoride and aluminum metal to produce AlF, and characterize the molecular beam using spectroscopy and buffer gas cooling.
result: They achieve a compact oven with high brightness, continuous output exceeding pulsed sources, and demonstrate rotational cooling to ~30 K using a cryogenic buffer gas cell.
conclusion: Continuous thermochemical sources of AlF are viable and can enable direct loading of magneto-optical traps, advancing molecular quantum science.

title: Analytical Response Functions For A Compressible Thin Fluid Layer With Odd Viscosity *
authors: Yuto Hosaka And Shigeyuki Komura Abdallah Daddi-Moussa-Ider
abstract: Fluids composed of chiral active components can exhibit odd viscosity, a property that breaks time-reversal and parity symmetries. We investigate the hydrodynamic response to monopole and dipole singularities in a compressible thin fluid layer with odd viscosity, supported by a conventional lubrication layer. Using the two-dimensional Green’s function in Fourier space, we derive analytical solutions for the flow and pressure fields. These solutions provide a detailed description of the hydrodynamic interactions governing the motion of colloidal particles and microswimmers in confined chiral fluids, offering insight into the role of odd viscosity in modifying particle dynamics and collective behavior. The derived results are directly applicable to modeling transport, control, and self-organization phenomena in active and chiral microfluidic systems.
tldr: This paper studies hydrodynamic response functions in a compressible thin fluid layer with odd viscosity, focusing on chiral active fluids.
motivation: Odd viscosity arises in chiral active fluids and affects particle dynamics and collective behavior; understanding its hydrodynamic effects is important for microfluidic applications.
method: The authors use two-dimensional Green's functions in Fourier space to derive analytical solutions for flow and pressure fields induced by monopole and dipole singularities.
result: Analytical expressions for the flow and pressure fields are obtained, showing how odd viscosity modifies hydrodynamic interactions.
conclusion: The results provide a framework for modeling transport and self-organization in chiral microfluidic systems.

title: Electron Spin Drift In Long-distance Plasma Wakefield Acceleration
authors: Ming Zeng And Dazhang Li Yilan Guo
abstract: Plasma based wakefield acceleration of polarized electron beams has recently attracted considerable research interest. Previous works have found the forced spin oscillation of electrons due to two-dimensional betatron oscillation in particle trajectory and discovered longitudinal depolarization mechanism in plasma wakefield. In this work, we present a three-dimensional analytical model for the electron spin dynamics and derive the evolution of polarization during long-distance plasma wakefield acceleration. Our analysis reveals several phenomena including a transverse rotational spin drift leading to depolarization, a reversal of the drift frequency, and a consequent recovery of polarization. This work can offer guidance on future plasma-based accelerators for polarized electron beams.
tldr: This paper presents a three-dimensional analytical model for electron spin dynamics in plasma wakefield acceleration, focusing on spin drift and polarization evolution.
motivation: Understanding and controlling electron spin polarization in plasma-based accelerators is important for future high-energy physics applications.
method: The authors develop a 3D analytical model for spin dynamics and derive the evolution of polarization during long-distance plasma wakefield acceleration.
result: They discover a transverse rotational spin drift leading to depolarization, a reversal of drift frequency, and a consequent recovery of polarization.
conclusion: The work provides guidance for designing plasma-based accelerators that preserve electron beam polarization.

title: Atomic-scale 3d Insights Into Heteroepitaxial Mechanisms In Hcp/fcc, Bcc/fcc, And Fcc/fcc Core–shell Nanoparticles
authors: Xilong Mu, Yao Zhang, Kang’an Wang, Haoyi Tang, Zhiheng Xie, Zezhou Li, Xuemin Cao, Peng He And Jihan Zhou
abstract: Heteroepitaxy on nanocrystals of diverse crystal structures—hexagonal close-packed (hcp), body-centered cubic (bcc), and face-centered cubic (fcc)—is a powerful approach for engineering atomic arrangements. However, the mechanisms by which interfacial defects and strain relaxation accommodate structural mismatch remain poorly understood at the three-dimensional (3D) atomic scale. Here, we use atomic-resolution electron tomography to determine the 3D atomic structures and reveal heteroepitaxial mechanisms in Pt-based core–shell nanoparticles with diverse crystal structures including hcp/fcc Ru@Pt, bcc/fcc PdCu@Pt, and fcc/fcc Ru@Pt. We have identified distinct heteroepitaxial modes in these model systems, each mitigating the structural mismatch within a single particle: mixed coherent/semi-coherent growth in hcp/fcc Ru@Pt, coherent growth with strain sharing between core and shell in bcc/fcc PdCu@Pt, and oriented growth combined with twin proliferation in decahedral fcc/fcc Ru@Pt. The various semi-coherent growth modes in the hcp/fcc nanoparticle yield a 3D dislocation network at a scale below 10 nm, interconnected by Lomer–Cottrell, Hirth, and Shockley dislocations. The key heteroepitaxial mechanisms in these examined systems are quantitatively validated by interfacial energies derived from molecular statics simulations. We anticipate these insights will inform the targeted design of interfacial structures and enable precise strain engineering in core–shell nanomaterials.
tldr: This paper uses atomic-resolution electron tomography to study heteroepitaxial mechanisms in core-shell nanoparticles with different crystal structures.
motivation: Understanding how interfacial defects and strain relaxation accommodate structural mismatch in heteroepitaxial nanoparticles is crucial for engineering atomic arrangements.
method: Atomic-resolution electron tomography was used to determine 3D atomic structures of Pt-based core-shell nanoparticles (hcp/fcc Ru@Pt, bcc/fcc PdCu@Pt, fcc/fcc Ru@Pt), combined with molecular statics simulations to validate interfacial energies.
result: Distinct heteroepitaxial modes were identified: mixed coherent/semi-coherent growth in hcp/fcc, coherent growth with strain sharing in bcc/fcc, and oriented growth with twin proliferation in fcc/fcc. A 3D dislocation network below 10 nm was observed.
conclusion: The insights inform targeted design of interfacial structures and precise strain engineering in core-shell nanomaterials.

tldr: This paper uses cryo-electron microscopy to determine the structure of the tip-link protein PCDH15, revealing a right-handed double-helix dimer architecture.

authors: Qi Suyichun Yangjiayan Renyu Zhanglijuan Fuqing Wuxu Hanyanmin Zhangahttps://ror.org/017zhmm22school Of Pharmacy, Health Science Center, Xi’an Jiaotong University, Xi’an 710061, PR Chinabstate Key Laboratory Of Shaanxi For Natural Medicines Research And Engineering, Xi’an 710061, PR China

SignificanceThe dedifferentiation of cancer cells is a major hallmark of malignancy and a challenge for therapy. Here, we reveal that hypoxia drives HCC dedifferentiation by actively eliminating peroxisomes, the organelles that help define liver cell ...
tldr: This paper investigates the role of Rnf126 in peroxisome elimination during hypoxia-driven dedifferentiation of hepatocellular carcinoma cells, proposing a redifferentiation therapy strategy.
motivation: Cancer cell dedifferentiation is a hallmark of malignancy and a therapeutic challenge; understanding the molecular mechanisms could lead to new treatments.
method: The study uses molecular biology techniques to show that hypoxia induces peroxisome degradation via Rnf126, and tests redifferentiation therapy in HCC models.
result: Rnf126 acts as a peroxisomal fate switch; its inhibition restores peroxisome function and promotes redifferentiation, reducing tumorigenicity.
conclusion: Targeting Rnf126-mediated peroxisome elimination may offer a novel therapeutic approach for hepatocellular carcinoma by inducing redifferentiation.
